ranking_reason: C supplies an exhaustive pairwise compatibility census and a small obstruction basis that protocol-by-protocol reading would not naturally yield. B quantifies an ontology gap but rests on manual coding. A reports a recognizable liquidation-stack compression without establishing that practitioners would find it surprising.
summary: C is the publishable result, but its strongest novelty is the exhaustive compatibility map and obstruction basis—not the unsurprising fact that union-closed positive constraints cannot cause pairwise-union failures.

findings.claim: The perpetuals category contains seven protocols, and six named protocols share the exact canonical omission {Ct, Ex, Li}.
findings.problem: The seventh perpetual is unnamed, so the bundle does not show whether this is a discriminating microstructure result or a selected common pattern. A competent practitioner could identify collateral testing, oracle use, and liquidation as recurring plumbing by reading these protocols.
findings.falsifier: Candidate A's opening paragraph lists only six of the asserted seven perpetuals; the seventh protocol's decomposition and canonical form would settle whether the pattern is selective.
findings.fix: Name and analyze the seventh perpetual, then show what the canonical-form proof establishes beyond an expert's direct functional decomposition.

findings.claim: Of 1,259 obligations, 689 are residue because the vocabulary has no name for them; positive theory therefore cannot be responsible for their noncoverage.
findings.problem: The causal statement is definitional once residue means 'has no name.' The quantitative result comes from hand-made decompositions and classifications, so the bundle does not establish that formalism contributed more than systematic manual taxonomy work.
findings.falsifier: Compare Candidate B's definition of residue with the opening description of the corpus as 'hand-made decompositions'; row-level obligation classifications and independent coding checks would settle whether the counts reveal a robust ontology boundary.
findings.fix: Present validation of the obligation coding and show a nontrivial consequence of the residue classification that cannot be obtained by merely comparing protocol descriptions with the vocabulary.

findings.claim: Every pairwise composition failure arms a prohibition; requirements, warrants, and grounding contribute none.
findings.problem: This attribution appears forced by the stated algebra: the positive models are union-closed, while admissibility adds prohibitions. It is therefore not an empirical discovery. The valuable result is instead the exhaustive 1,830-pair census, its topology, and reduction to 15 arcs and 10 elements.
findings.falsifier: The abstract passage stating that positive-constraint models form a complete lattice under union and admissibility intersects that class with prohibitions settles the attribution's inevitability.
findings.fix: Reframe C around the exhaustive compatibility matrix and compact obstruction certificates, and label prohibition-only failure as a theorem-driven sanity check.

findings.claim: Of 1,830 pairs, 1,645 compose to an admissible set and 185 do not.
findings.problem: Here composition means union of vocabulary subsets, not demonstrated operational interoperability between deployed protocols. Without that qualification, the wording invites a stronger and more interesting interpretation than the evidence supports.
findings.falsifier: The abstract's definition of a protocol as a finite vocabulary subset, read against Candidate C's phrase 'compose to an admissible set,' fixes the modeled meaning of composition.
findings.fix: Call these 'pairwise unions admissible in the model' and reserve operational composition claims for separately validated semantics.

strongest_candidate_argument: C turns scattered protocol descriptions into an exhaustive compatibility graph with checkable failure certificates and a compact obstruction basis, a global result unavailable from reading any protocol in isolation.
dissent_note: A coverage-focused reviewer may prefer B's scale, but without coding validation its headline measures annotation practice as much as formal expressivity.
